That is not a party political point; it is a point about trust. Local authorities across Wales planned multi-year programmes on the assumption that funding levels would be maintained, and many of those programmes support exactly the kind of community infrastructure, skills training and business support that the Minister says he wants to see thrive. If the funding settlement falls short, those plans will simply not happen, and it will be communities in the Valleys and in rural mid-Wales who pay the price, not Whitehall.

I would also ask the Minister to clarify how decisions on individual projects will be made and by whom. One of the great strengths of the old structural funds system, whatever its faults, was that it built in a genuine partnership between the Welsh Government, local government and the European Commission, with agreed regional strategies that reflected local priorities rather than priorities set centrally in London. If the shared prosperity fund simply becomes another vehicle for Whitehall departments to bypass the Welsh Government and deal directly with local councils, we risk losing that coherence, and we risk seeing money spent on projects that look good in a press release but do not fit into any wider strategic plan for the Welsh economy.

Finally, I would welcome an assurance from the Minister that the promised UK-wide shared prosperity fund will not simply reproduce the Barnett formula's well known weaknesses. Wales has particular needs arising from its historic reliance on industries in long-term decline, and any funding formula that ignores that will fail the very communities it is supposed to help.

We know from experience with other trade agreements that these investor-state dispute mechanisms can be used by large multinational corporations to challenge legitimate public policy decisions, whether those relate to environmental protection, public health or the rights of Indigenous peoples to be consulted on projects that affect their traditional territories. We have seen cases in other jurisdictions where governments have been forced to pay enormous settlements simply because they tried to strengthen environmental regulations or protect drinking water. That is not hypothetical; it is documented history, and it should give every member of this House pause.

I am glad that some of the more egregious provisions have been narrowed in the new agreement, but I do not think we can simply declare victory and move on. We need to ensure that any dispute resolution mechanism that remains in place cannot be used to override the democratic will of Parliament or of provincial legislatures, particularly when it comes to environmental assessments and consultation with Indigenous communities, which are constitutionally protected rights, not optional courtesies.

I would also ask the government to be transparent about how these provisions were negotiated and what assessments were done of their potential impact on our ability to legislate in the public interest. Canadians deserve to know whether we traded away meaningful sovereignty in exchange for market access, and if so, what exactly we received in return. This is not an abstract debate about trade law; it is about whether a future government will have the freedom to say no to a pipeline, no to a mine, or no to a development that threatens a watershed, without facing a multi-million dollar lawsuit from a foreign corporation.

We owe it to the Indigenous nations who have fought for decades to have their voices heard in these processes to get this right, and I will be pressing the government for further clarity as this agreement moves through ratification.

I want to address directly the concerns that have been raised about the economic support available. The Chancellor has extended the furlough scheme, and grants will be available to businesses that are required to close, but I accept that for many self-employed people and for those who have fallen through the gaps of previous support schemes, this remains an incredibly difficult time. I will continue to press the Treasury on this point, because economic hardship is not a price we should ask some communities to pay disproportionately while others are protected.

I also want to acknowledge the extraordinary sacrifices that have already been made. Families have missed birthdays, funerals and weddings. Businesses that took a lifetime to build have been mothballed. Key workers have gone above and beyond what anyone could reasonably ask of them. It is precisely because of those sacrifices that we cannot afford to let the virus run unchecked now, undoing everything that has already been achieved.

I would ask the House to support these measures, painful as they are, because the alternative — an uncontrolled surge in infections — would cost far more in lives and in livelihoods than the restrictions we are debating today.

Nobody in this House wants to see people wrongly branded as criminals for minor missteps, but equally, nobody in this House should want to see genuine harassment go unpunished simply because we were too cautious in drafting the law.

What matters is proportionality, and what matters is that the guidance which accompanies this legislation is clear enough that employers, tribunals and the police all understand where the line sits. I have heard from constituents on both sides of this issue: from women who have experienced workplace harassment and felt that nothing was ever done about it, and from employers who are anxious that well-intentioned policies could be applied in ways that damage careers over misunderstandings. Both concerns are legitimate, and both deserve to be addressed in the detail of how this law is implemented, not just in its headline provisions.

I would ask the Minister to confirm that there will be proper training for those responsible for enforcing these provisions, because legislation is only as good as its implementation. A law that looks proportionate on paper can still be applied unevenly if those enforcing it do not have clear guidance and adequate resources.

I would also urge the Minister to consider how smaller employers, who may not have dedicated human resources teams, will be supported to understand their obligations. It is easy to legislate for large organisations with compliance departments; it is harder, but more important, to ensure that a small business with five employees understands exactly what is expected of it too. I look forward to hearing more about how the Government intend to bridge that gap.

I would ask the Minister to provide a clear timeline for implementation of the review's findings, and to commit to regular updates to this House on progress. Families in Donegal have waited long enough. They deserve to see change, not just be told that change is coming.

We in this House have spent years now debating the minutiae of withdrawal agreements, backstops and future frameworks, often losing sight of the fact that beyond these walls, businesses have been forced to make decisions with imperfect information, families have faced genuine uncertainty about their rights, and our reputation as a reliable negotiating partner has been tested time and again.

I do not say this to relitigate the referendum result, which this House has accepted and which the country voted for. I say it because how we leave matters just as much as whether we leave. A disorderly departure, driven by brinkmanship rather than preparation, would visit real and lasting harm on ordinary people who have no voice in these negotiations beyond the vote they already cast.

I would urge the Government, even at this late stage, to prioritise clarity over theatre, and substance over slogans. The stakes are too high, and the historical parallels, however imperfect, too instructive, for us to sleepwalk into an outcome that none of us, on reflection, would actually choose.

I understand the intention behind that amendment, and I have some sympathy with it, because nobody in this House wants to see tenants penalised twice for the same breach.

However, I would gently push back on the suggestion that the current drafting creates that risk. The Bill as it stands already provides that landlords and agents may only recover the actual loss they have suffered as a result of a genuine breach of contract, verified where necessary by evidence such as receipts or invoices. That is a meaningful safeguard against the kind of speculative or punitive charging that gave rise to calls for this legislation in the first place.

What we must avoid, in trying to close one loophole, is opening another. If we drafted the Bill in a way that prevented landlords from recovering genuine, documented losses — for example, the cost of repairing a broken window or replacing a lost key — we would create a perverse incentive that could ultimately push up rents generally, as landlords built the risk of unrecoverable costs into their pricing across their entire portfolio. That would harm the very tenants this Bill is designed to protect.

I would therefore ask the hon. Member for Great Grimsby to consider withdrawing the amendment, on the basis that the existing drafting already achieves the balance she seeks, while I commit to keeping this issue under review as the Bill's provisions take effect, and to returning to the House if evidence emerges that landlords are, in practice, using contractual breach clauses as a back door to reintroduce the fees this legislation was designed to abolish.

What makes this debate urgent is not simply the immediate hardship faced by workers and companies in this sector, though that hardship is very real. I want to be clear that this is not simply a call for unconditional bailouts. Any support provided by government must come with conditions attached — protections for workers, commitments to environmental responsibility, and a genuine plan for how this industry adapts to a lower-carbon future. We cannot use this crisis as an excuse to prop up business models that were already unsustainable before COVID-19 arrived. But we also cannot pretend that an industry critical to our national economic recovery does not deserve serious, thoughtful support during an unprecedented global shock.

When we talk about asylum seekers who cross into Canada between official ports of entry, we are talking about individuals exercising a right recognized under both Canadian and international law — the right to seek asylum, regardless of the manner of one's arrival, provided that a claim is made promptly and in good faith. That is a principle enshrined in the 1951 Refugee Convention, to which Canada is a signatory, and it is a principle that has served us well, allowing this country to offer protection to people fleeing genuine persecution.

That is entirely separate from questions about our broader immigration system, processing backlogs, or the mechanisms by which economic migrants apply to come to this country through regular channels. Those are legitimate subjects for debate, and I welcome scrutiny of how efficiently our system operates. But when members opposite blur the line between asylum seekers exercising a legal right and other categories of migration, they do a disservice to the complexity of this issue, and frankly, they do a disservice to the vulnerable people whose claims are being processed.

I would ask my colleagues to be precise in their language going forward, because precision matters here. The words we use in this Chamber shape public perception, and public perception, in turn, shapes how asylum seekers are treated in their communities. We owe it to those who have fled genuine danger to get this distinction right, every single time we discuss it.

We know from international evidence, particularly from jurisdictions that have gone further than we have, that removing alcohol sponsorship from sport does not spell financial ruin for sporting bodies, as some in the industry like to claim. I would ask the Minister of State to update the House on where things stand with the broader public health alcohol strategy, and specifically whether there are any plans to extend the current restrictions to cover a wider range of sporting events and broadcast contexts. We have made a start, but a start is not the same as a solution, and I am concerned that momentum on this issue has slowed considerably in recent times.

I would also note that sporting bodies themselves are not monolithic on this issue. Many within the GAA, for instance, have voiced concern about the messages sent by alcohol branding at underage and juvenile fixtures in particular, and I think this House should be listening closely to those voices rather than simply deferring to the commercial interests of the drinks industry, however significant its sponsorship contributions may currently be.

It is one thing to say that we respect the European Convention on Human Rights; it is quite another to build legislation that gives full and practical effect to that commitment.

That is why I have tabled amendments today that would place these principles on a statutory footing, rather than leaving them to guidance or to ministerial discretion. If the Government genuinely believe, as they say they do, that these obligations are already met by the Bill as drafted, then accepting these amendments should cost them nothing. If, on the other hand, they resist putting these principles into the text of the Bill itself, the House is entitled to ask why.

I do not say this to score political points. I say it because I have sat in this Chamber and heard commitments given in good faith that were later quietly abandoned when circumstances changed. Writing our obligations into law, rather than relying on the good intentions of whoever happens to hold ministerial office, is the only way to guarantee that these principles endure.

Once thermal runaway begins, the cell generates its own heat faster than it can dissipate it, triggering a self-sustaining chemical reaction that can reach temperatures well in excess of what conventional fire suppression methods are designed to handle. That is why lithium-ion battery fires are so difficult to extinguish, and why they can reignite hours, or even days, after they appear to have been put out.

This matters enormously for the policy question before us today, because the growth in lithium-ion battery use — in electric vehicles, in home energy storage systems, in e-bikes and e-scooters, and in countless consumer electronics — has vastly outpaced the development of regulations and safety standards designed to manage this risk. Fire services across the country have reported a sharp rise in incidents involving these batteries, and in many cases, they are dealing with a hazard that simply did not exist in anything like the same volume a decade ago.

I want to be clear that I am not arguing against the transition to battery-powered technology, which is essential to our decarbonisation goals. What I am arguing is that this transition must be accompanied by proper regulation covering manufacturing standards, safe disposal and recycling, and clear guidance for consumers on charging practices, particularly for the cheaper, unregulated products increasingly imported and sold online with minimal safety testing.

I would ask the Minister to set out what assessment has been made of current regulatory gaps, and what timeline exists for closing them, because every month of delay increases the risk to households, to firefighters, and to communities living near storage and disposal facilities.

It speaks directly to whether Canadians can trust that decisions about who is or is not prosecuted are made independently, free from political interference, regardless of a company's size or its connections.

I would ask the government House leader today: what concrete changes have been made to prevent this kind of interference from happening again, beyond simply hoping that Canadians will forget?

That episode taught us something important: that in negotiations of this magnitude, where trust between partners is already fragile, careless or ill-judged remarks carry consequences far beyond the immediate news cycle.

I raise this not to dwell on past mistakes but because it bears directly on how we approach the Brexit negotiations going forward. Ireland's position has been, and must remain, one of unwavering solidarity with our EU partners, precisely because that solidarity is what has secured us the protections we need — protections for the Good Friday Agreement, for the all-island economy, and for the rights of citizens across this island who never voted to leave the European Union in the first place.

We must also be honest that the coming months will require extraordinary diplomatic skill. The negotiations on the future relationship are, in many ways, more complex than the withdrawal agreement itself, because they touch on the entire architecture of how goods, services and people move between Britain, Ireland and the wider Union. Any faltering in our approach, any sense that we are freelancing rather than working in lockstep with Brussels, risks undermining the very protections we have fought so hard to secure.

I will now turn to the specific questions raised about Northern Ireland in the next group, but I wanted to set out clearly why our continued unity with our European partners remains, in my view, the single most important factor in protecting Ireland's interests throughout what remains of this process.

This represents a genuine shift in how we approach housing policy in this country, moving beyond an over-reliance on the private rental market and towards a model where the State takes direct responsibility for providing secure, affordable homes at below-market rents.

I want to acknowledge that for too long, successive governments allowed the State's capacity to deliver housing directly to wither, leaving us overly dependent on a private market that, left to its own devices, will always prioritise the highest possible return over affordability or security of tenure. The programmes we are now delivering represent a deliberate and necessary correction to that approach.

That said, I do not want to stand here and suggest that the scale of what we are delivering yet matches the scale of the crisis facing so many families and individuals across this country. Waiting lists remain far too long, and I hear regularly from constituents who are working full time, sometimes in more than one job, and who still cannot find a home they can afford within a reasonable commute of their employment.

What gives me confidence that we are moving in the right direction is not just the number of homes delivered so far, but the pipeline of projects now in planning and construction, which represents the largest sustained State investment in affordable and social housing delivery in a generation. I would ask this House to judge this Government not on any single year's output, but on the trajectory we have now established, and I am confident that trajectory will continue to accelerate as these programmes mature.

We have seen too many cases where good intentions at the top of a Department fail to translate into fair treatment for the individual sitting across the table, or in this case, across a telephone line, from an assessor.

That is precisely why I want to focus my remarks today on something concrete rather than abstract: the impact of rising energy costs on households in my constituency who have no realistic alternative but to absorb these increases, month after month, out of already stretched budgets. I have heard from pensioners choosing between heating one room of their home and leaving the rest cold, from young families rationing hot water, from small business owners watching their margins evaporate under the weight of commercial energy tariffs that have risen far faster than they can pass on to already squeezed customers.

If this House is to justify the scepticism my own family expressed this weekend, we need to show, through concrete action rather than further debate for its own sake, that we understand the scale of what ordinary people are being asked to bear, and that we are prepared to act accordingly, and urgently.

I would also point to the broader package of measures the European Union and its allies, including the United Kingdom, have coordinated on economic and diplomatic fronts. I want to be candid with my hon. I would also emphasise the importance of coordination with our allies on enforcement, because sanctions that exist on paper but are inconsistently applied across jurisdictions provide far too many opportunities for evasion. We have seen sophisticated efforts by sanctioned individuals and entities to route transactions through third countries or to exploit gaps between different national sanctions regimes, and closing those gaps requires sustained diplomatic engagement, not simply the initial announcement of new measures.

I can assure my hon. Friend and the House that this Government remains committed to keeping the full range of tools at our disposal under continuous review, and to working closely with our European and transatlantic partners to ensure that the pressure applied to Russia, and to those who enable its aggression, continues to intensify rather than plateau.

We know, from the evidence before us and from the lived experience of millions of Canadians, that the current patchwork of income supports fails to provide anything close to a dignified standard of living. People with disabilities, seniors on fixed incomes, and low-wage workers are being forced to choose between rent and groceries, between medication and heat, in one of the wealthiest countries on earth. That is not a failure of individual effort; it is a failure of policy choices made repeatedly by successive governments that have prioritised austerity and incrementalism over genuine, transformative investment in the social safety net.

The NDP has long called for a guaranteed livable income, one that would ensure no Canadian falls below a basic threshold of dignity regardless of their circumstances. We have been told, repeatedly, that this is too expensive, too complicated, too far outside the realm of political feasibility. And yet we found the political will, almost overnight, to provide emergency income support during the pandemic, proving conclusively that the barrier to acting on poverty has never been genuine impossibility. It has been a lack of political will.

I would ask this House to consider today's motion not as an isolated gesture, but as a first step towards building the political consensus needed to finally close the dignity gap that continues to define far too many Canadians' daily experience of this wealthy country.

That means, above all, a serious and sustained investment in skills training, not as an afterthought bolted onto existing further education provision, but as a central pillar of our economic recovery strategy. Too many workers displaced from sectors hit hardest by the pandemic — hospitality, retail, parts of the events industry — currently have no clear, accessible pathway to retrain for the growing sectors of our economy: green energy, digital technology, advanced manufacturing.

I would ask the Minister to set out what specific, additional funding will be made available for adult retraining, distinct from the existing apprenticeship levy arrangements, which primarily benefit younger people entering the workforce for the first time rather than experienced workers seeking to pivot into new sectors mid-career. We need a genuine offer for the forty-five-year-old former hospitality worker who wants to retrain in renewable energy installation, not just for the eighteen-year-old school leaver.

I would also emphasise the regional dimension of this challenge, because the sectors best positioned for growth are not evenly distributed across the country, and any national retraining strategy must be paired with genuine investment in regional infrastructure and connectivity, so that retrained workers actually have access to the jobs their new skills qualify them for, rather than finding those opportunities concentrated in parts of the country far from where they live.

I would ask the Minister to set out what specific engagement takes place between the UK Government and the National Assembly on Welsh language policy, to ensure that decisions made at Westminster, even in reserved areas, are made with full awareness of their potential impact on the language's continued revival, rather than as an afterthought considered only once concerns are raised after the fact.

Ultimately, I share the underlying ambition that has driven Welsh language policy across successive Assembly administrations, and while the primary responsibility and the primary tools rightly sit in Cardiff Bay, I do not believe that means Westminster should be entirely silent, or entirely passive, when it comes to supporting a language that is such a fundamental part of Welsh identity and culture.

I want to be absolutely clear about what decriminalisation means and, equally importantly, what it does not mean. It does not mean the removal of clinical safeguards, gestational limits, or the professional standards that govern how abortion care is provided in this country. Doctors will continue to exercise their clinical judgment within a regulated framework; nothing in this Bill removes that responsibility or that oversight. What changes is simply this: a woman who makes this decision, and the clinician who provides her care within the existing 24-week limit, will no longer face the possibility of criminal prosecution for doing so.

I know that this issue provokes strong feelings across this House, and I respect the sincerity of those who hold different views from my own. But I would ask colleagues to consider the practical reality of what criminalisation has meant in practice: not fewer abortions, but abortions pursued in circumstances of greater fear, greater secrecy, and in the most extreme cases, greater danger, as women who feel they cannot approach the formal healthcare system safely seek alternatives that carry far greater risk to their health.

This Bill brings our law into closer alignment with how healthcare is actually delivered and experienced by women across this country, replacing the shadow of criminal law with a framework built around clinical safeguards and genuine patient care, and I commend it to the House.

I raise this not primarily out of concern for the inconvenience such a scenario might cause to Members of this House, who are, after all, no more deserving of exemption from the law than any other citizen. I raise it because the scenario illustrates a broader point about the sweeping nature of the powers this Bill creates: powers so broad, and so loosely defined, that even those debating and voting on this very legislation cannot say with confidence whether they themselves might fall within its scope.

If we are not confident that these powers are proportionate and clearly bounded enough to explain their application even to ourselves, sitting in this Chamber with full access to the Bill's drafters and full opportunity for scrutiny, how can we possibly expect ordinary members of the public, who will have none of those advantages, to understand when and how these powers might be used against them? I would urge the Minister to address this question directly, rather than dismissing it as far-fetched.
